pages.text: Olympia is a small town in Greece. It is famous for a nearby old site. This place was a major religious center in ancient times. The ancient Olympic Games were held there every four years from the eighth century BC to the fourth century AD.

Throughout classical antiquity, this Panhellenic religious sanctuary hosted the ancient Olympic Games every four years from the eighth century BC to the fourth century AD.

pages.text: Abolitionism is the political movement to end slavery and free enslaved people around the world. This important movement grew stronger in the western world during the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

pages.text: France was the first country to fully outlaw slavery in 1315, though it was still used in its colonies. Later, Spain banned slavery for indigenous people in 1542. Japan also abolished chattel slavery starting in 1590.

A1-A2.headline: The Story of the Atlantic Slave Trade

pages.text: The Atlantic slave trade involved moving enslaved people from Africa to the Americas. This trade lasted for many centuries, starting in the fifteenth century and continuing into the nineteenth century. Ships from both Europe and the New World carried these captive people across the ocean.
pages.caption: Reproduction of a handbill advertising a slave auction in Charleston, British Province of South Carolina, in 1769

evidence.articleCaption: Reproduction of a handbill advertising a slave auction in Charleston, British Province of South Carolina, in 1769

pages.text: Most of the people who were taken came from Central and West Africa. Slave merchants in Africa sold these captives to buyers. European traders mostly purchased them on the coast instead of capturing them through raids. Some nations built forts or used their ships as bases to wait for cargoes.
pages.caption: A map of the Spanish Empire (red) and Portuguese Empires (blue) in the period of their personal union (1581–1640)

evidence.articleCaption: A map of the Spanish Empire (red) and Portuguese Empires (blue) in the period of their personal union (1581–1640)

pages.text: Europeans conquered lands in the Americas, but the native population shrank because of diseases. European workers were reluctant to emigrate there in large numbers. To solve this labor shortage, colonists turned to bringing enslaved people from sub-Saharan Africa to work the land.
pages.caption: Noah curses Ham by Gustave Doré – the curse of Ham was used as a justification to enslave Africans.

pages.text: Enslaved Africans were sold to work on plantations growing crops like sugar, cotton, and tobacco. They also worked in mines and did construction. Over time, this system changed into chattel slavery. Enslaved people and their children became the legal property of their owners, bought and sold at markets.
pages.caption: Elmina Castle on the Guinea coast, present-day Ghana, was built in 1482 by Portuguese traders. Its primary purpose was trading in gold, but when the outward slave trade from the Gold Coast began, it was used in the slave trade. The Gold Coast was a late entrant to the outward slave trade (though there was an inward trade to supply workers in the gold mines).

pages.text: Seven main nations carried out most of this trade, usually bringing slaves to their own colonies. Millions of Africans were loaded onto ships for the journey. Tragically, many people died at sea before reaching the Americas. Near the start of the nineteenth century, various governments began to ban the trade.

B1-B2.headline: History and Impact of Transatlantic Slaving

pages.text: The transatlantic slave trade was a massive historical movement operated by slave ships from Europe and the New World. It involved the forced transportation of enslaved African people to the Americas. Initiated by Europeans establishing a coastal trade in the fifteenth century, this practice persisted well into the nineteenth century, often utilizing the triangular trade route.
pages.caption: Reproduction of a handbill advertising a slave auction in Charleston, British Province of South Carolina, in 1769

evidence.articleCaption: Reproduction of a handbill advertising a slave auction in Charleston, British Province of South Carolina, in 1769

pages.text: The majority of the transported individuals originated from Central and West Africa. Rather than engaging in widespread raiding, Europeans typically purchased their captives from local African slave merchants. Traders gathered people using coastal forts or by utilizing their own anchored ships as floating bases, which often meant longer periods of confinement for the captives before departure.
pages.caption: A map of the Spanish Empire (red) and Portuguese Empires (blue) in the period of their personal union (1581–1640)

evidence.articleCaption: A map of the Spanish Empire (red) and Portuguese Empires (blue) in the period of their personal union (1581–1640)

pages.text: European conquest in the Americas created an urgent demand for a workforce. Because the indigenous population was shrinking due to European diseases and few Europeans were willing to emigrate, colonists faced severe labor shortages. The solution mirrored earlier practices used on island sugar plantations: importing enslaved people from sub-Saharan Africa.
pages.caption: Noah curses Ham by Gustave Doré – the curse of Ham was used as a justification to enslave Africans.

evidence.articleCaption: Noah curses Ham by Gustave Doré – the curse of Ham was used as a justification to enslave Africans.

pages.text: In the Americas, enslaved Africans labored on vast plantations producing coffee, tobacco, sugar, and cotton, as well as working in mines and construction. By the mid-seventeenth century, this labor transformed into a legal racial caste system of chattel slavery. Individuals and their offspring were treated as merchandise and property, valued according to health and expected productivity.

The Gold Coast was a late entrant to the outward slave trade (though there was an inward trade to supply workers in the gold mines).

pages.text: Portugal, Britain, Spain, France, the Netherlands, the United States, and Denmark were the primary trading nations. Estimates suggest that about 12.75 million Africans were loaded onto ships, with up to two million perishing during the journey. Near the beginning of the nineteenth century, governments began banning the trade, though illegal smuggling persisted.

C1-C2.headline: Dynamics of the Transatlantic Slave Trade

pages.text: The transatlantic slave trade entailed the systematic maritime transportation of enslaved Africans to the Americas by European and New World merchants. Emerging from fifteenth-century European coastal initiatives, the trade persisted for centuries, frequently incorporating the triangular trade route and the Middle Passage during its earlier operational phases.
pages.caption: Reproduction of a handbill advertising a slave auction in Charleston, British Province of South Carolina, in 1769

evidence.articleCaption: Reproduction of a handbill advertising a slave auction in Charleston, British Province of South Carolina, in 1769

pages.text: Originating predominantly from Central and West Africa, the captive populations were generally acquired through purchase from regional African merchants rather than direct European raiding. While the Portuguese constructed barracoons to assemble captives, northern Europeans often utilized their vessels as floating bases. pages.text: Romanticism was a big artistic and intellectual movement in Europe. It started near the end of the 18th century. The movement focused on nature, imagination, and personal feelings. People wanted this change after the Age of Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution.

evidence.articleCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, 1818

pages.text: Romantic artists and thinkers did not like old social rules. They believed in individualism. They thought passion and intuition were very important to understand the world. Beauty was about strong emotional responses, not just simple forms.
pages.caption: Eugène Delacroix, Death of Sardanapalus, 1827, taking its Orientalist subject from a play by Lord Byron

pages.text: The movement loved the Middle Ages. Writers and artists saw this time as an era of chivalry and heroes. They liked the close relationship between humans and nature. This was very different from their modern industrial society.

evidence.articleCaption: Philipp Otto Runge, The Morning, 1808

pages.text: For most of the Western world, Romanticism was at its peak from approximately 1800 to 1850. The movement started with ideas from an earlier German movement called Sturm und Drang. Events and ideologies of the French Revolution also directly influenced the movement and its early participants.
pages.caption: William Blake, The Little Girl Found, from Songs of Innocence and Experience, 1794

pages.text: In literature, important English poets like William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge wrote famous works. The publication of Lyrical Ballads in 1798 is often seen as the start of the movement in England. Their poems explored nature and human feelings.

After the main movement ended, its thoughts and art influenced many fields like philosophy, politics, and environmentalism. Even today, the ideas of Romanticism continue to impact the world, though modern uses of the word can be quite different.

Originating in Europe toward the end of the 18th century, Romanticism was a major artistic and intellectual movement. It arose as a response to both the Age of Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution, advocating strongly for subjectivity, imagination, and a deep appreciation of nature.

pages.text: Romanticists rejected contemporary social conventions in favor of individualism. They argued that passion and intuition were crucial for understanding the world. pages.text: The movement showed a distinct fondness for the Middle Ages, viewing the era as a time of chivalry, heroism, and an organic human relationship with the environment. This idealization contrasted sharply with the alienation and environmental degradation caused by industrial society.

pages.text: Historians generally agree that Romanticism peaked between 1800 and 1850. Its roots trace back to the German Counter-Enlightenment movement known as Sturm und Drang. Early romantics were also directly influenced by the ideals and events of the French Revolution.

pages.text: In English literature, figures like William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge helped launch the movement with the 1798 publication of Lyrical Ballads. While some early writers were viewed as marginal radicals, their focus on nature and intense feelings transformed poetry.

Although the movement largely dispersed by the time of World War I, Romantic thought left an enduring legacy. Its influence spread across art, music, speculative fiction, philosophy, politics, and environmentalism, continuing to shape culture to the present day.

Emerging in Europe toward the late 18th century, Romanticism functioned as a comprehensive artistic and intellectual movement. It developed primarily as a cultural reaction against the scientific rationalization of the Age of Enlightenment and the socioeconomic shifts of the Industrial Revolution.

pages.text: Literary milestones such as the 1798 publication of Lyrical Ballads marked key developments in England, where foundational figures championed authentic emotional expression. Writers prioritized the subjective autonomy of the artist, famously described by William Wordsworth as the overflow of powerful feelings.

Following its eventual dispersion around the onset of World War I, Romantic ideology exerted a pervasive influence on Western civilization. Its long-term impact permeated diverse domains including speculative fiction, political theory, philosophy, and environmentalism, enduring into contemporary times.

Originating in Europe toward the end of the 18th century, Romanticism was a major artistic and intellectual movement. It arose as a response to both the Age of Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution, advocating strongly for subjectivity, imagination, and a deep appreciation of nature.

A1-A2.headline: Leonardo da Vinci, Artist and Inventor

pages.text: Leonardo da Vinci lived from 1452 to 1519. He was a famous Italian artist who also studied science, engineering, and nature. Today, he is known around the world for paintings like the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper, but he also spent much of his life working as an inventor and engineer.
pages.caption: Vitruvian Man, c. 1490

evidence.articleCaption: Vitruvian Man, c. 1490

pages.text: During his lifetime, Leonardo did not go to a university and had no formal training in Latin or math. Because of this, other scholars largely ignored his science studies. Instead, he used his eyes as his main tool, watching the world closely and recording details in his personal journals.
pages.caption: Investigating the motion of the arm

pages.text: Leonardo wrote and drew in his journals almost every day. He used his left hand and wrote in mirror script, which can be hard to read. These pages show his deep interest in how things worked, from flying machines and bridges to human anatomy and the movement of water.
pages.caption: The Lady with an Ermine

pages.text: To better understand the body, Leonardo dissected human corpses. He also studied animals like cows, monkeys, and frogs to compare their structures with humans. His drawings of bones, muscles, and organs helped him create more realistic and powerful works of art.

pages.text: Leonardo designed many machines that were far ahead of his time. Although some ideas were too costly to build, his detailed drawings included early concepts for things like helicopters and parachutes. His careful observations linked art and science together in a remarkable way.

B1-B2.headline: The Scientific Mind of Leonardo da Vinci

pages.text: Leonardo da Vinci is celebrated globally for masterpieces like the Mona Lisa, yet his genius extended far beyond painting. As an Italian polymath of the Renaissance, he immersed himself in diverse fields ranging from geometry and hydrodynamics to mechanics, anatomy, and civil engineering.

pages.text: Lacking formal university education and knowledge of Latin, Leonardo relied primarily on intense visual observation rather than academic theory. His investigative processes are preserved in numerous journals, where he recorded daily thoughts, plans, and observations using his left hand in mirror script.

pages.text: For Leonardo, art and science were closely intertwined. His artistic training informed his scientific approach, while his scientific studies helped him render the physical world with extraordinary precision. pages.text: Leonardo advanced human anatomical knowledge through meticulous dissections of human corpses at various hospitals, collaborating with medical professionals. He also dissected animals such as monkeys, frogs, and cows to compare their anatomical structures with those of humans, recording his findings in detailed drawings.

pages.text: His notebooks contain thousands of pages featuring advanced mechanical designs and technical drawings. He conceived concepts for parachutes, helicopters, and armored vehicles, and understood complex principles like friction and leverage. Although many ideas proved impractical or too costly during his lifetime, his technical drawings pioneered modern drafting techniques.

C1-C2.headline: Empirical Observation and Invention in the Renaissance

pages.text: Epitomizing the Renaissance ideal, Leonardo da Vinci integrated artistic mastery with extensive inquiries into diverse disciplines such as hydrodynamics, geometry, and mechanical engineering. While his paintings achieved widespread renown, his contemporary employment relied primarily on his aptitude for invention and engineering.
pages.caption: Vitruvian Man, c. 1490

pages.text: Operating without formal university training or proficiency in Latin, Leonardo approached natural philosophy through rigorous empirical observation rather than scholastic orthodoxy. His investigative methodologies relied almost exclusively on visual scrutiny, documenting his daily analyses, technical plans, and reflective notes in mirror script within surviving journals.

pages.text: During the Renaissance, artistic and scientific pursuits were mutually reinforcing. Leonardo leveraged anatomical and optical insights to refine his artistic rendering. This synthesis is exemplified by the Vitruvian Man, which bridges artistic proportion with human anatomical study to reflect the concepts of microcosm and macrocosm.

pages.text: To attain precise anatomical knowledge, Leonardo conducted systematic human dissections across multiple Italian hospitals in collaboration with medical practitioners. Complementing this, comparative anatomical studies involving various animal species allowed him to contrast structural morphologies through meticulous, illustrative sketches.

pages.text: Spanning over five thousand notebook pages, Leonardo's technical studies anticipated modern mechanical principles, including advanced leverage, gearing, friction, and aerodynamics.
